title: How Concrete Sets and How It Fails
topic: the chemistry of Portland cement and concrete
paragraphs: By weight, people make more concrete than any other manufactured thing, and most never ask how it works.
Concrete does not dry into a solid.
It grows one.
The story starts in a quarry and a kiln.
The binder in ordinary concrete is Portland cement, made by burning roughly four parts limestone to one part clay or shale.
Limestone is calcium carbonate, and the clay supplies silica, alumina, and iron.
That mixture, called raw meal, goes into the kiln, and near nine hundred degrees Celsius the limestone gives up its carbon dioxide and becomes calcium oxide, or quicklime.
This step is called calcination, and it is the source of both the usefulness and the trouble of cement.
Farther down the kiln, at about fourteen hundred and fifty degrees, the quicklime and the clay's silica and alumina fuse into new compounds and emerge as dark gravel sized nodules called clinker.
Four phases matter.
Tricalcium silicate, called alite, makes up half to two thirds of the clinker and does most of the early work.
Dicalcium silicate, called belite, is about a fifth and works slowly.
Tricalcium aluminate and a calcium aluminoferrite fill out the rest, the first alarmingly quick to react and the second responsible for the gray color.
Clinker is cooled and ground finer than flour, with three to five percent gypsum by mass ground in.
The gypsum is not filler.
Without it the tricalcium aluminate would react within minutes and seize the batch into a useless stiff mass, called flash set.
Sulfate from the gypsum reaches the aluminate first and builds needles of ettringite around each grain, slowing the aluminate and buying the hours a crew needs to place the batch.
Add water and the real reaction begins.
The calcium silicates react with the water and precipitate a new solid, a calcium silicate hydrate that chemists write as C-S-H and everyone else calls the glue.
It grows outward from every cement grain as a tangle of sheets and fibers that locks sand and stone together.
The same reaction releases calcium hydroxide, a mineral called portlandite, which is not much of a glue but matters enormously later.
The two silicates set the pace.
Alite hydrates quickly and supplies most of the strength gained in the first week.
Belite hydrates slowly and keeps adding strength for months and years, so a structure quietly gets stronger long after the forms come off.
A cement heavier in belite runs cool and gains late, an advantage in a massive dam, where the heat of reaction would crack the mass as it cooled.
Here the common intuition fails.
Concrete does not harden by drying out.
Water is a reactant, built into the C-S-H, and hydration stops when the water runs out, whether or not the surface looks dry.
Curing, on a site, means keeping the water in: misting, wet burlap, ponding.
Concrete that is still green, soft enough to take a thumbprint and not yet carrying load, is most easily ruined by a hot dry afternoon.
Crews routinely add more water than hydration needs, because a wetter mix is easier to place, and every extra measure leaves a capillary pore when it evaporates.
Those pores are where strength goes, and they are the roads by which everything that later attacks the concrete gets in.
The kiln, meanwhile, has a problem no engineer can design away.
Roughly half a tonne of carbon dioxide leaves the limestone for every tonne of clinker, purely as stoichiometry, before any fuel is counted.
Firing the kiln and grinding the product push the total near eight tenths of a tonne.
More than half of cement's emissions are therefore chemical rather than combustion: the carbon was in the rock, and making cement means taking it out.
Cement production is commonly put at seven or eight percent of human carbon dioxide emissions, well above aviation.
Concrete is strong in compression and weak in tension, so it is nearly always cast around steel bars.
The pairing works partly because both expand and contract with temperature at almost the same rate, and partly because of the portlandite.
The pore water in hardened concrete is saturated with calcium hydroxide and alkali, giving it a pH between about twelve and a half and thirteen and a half.
In liquid that alkaline, steel grows a thin, tight oxide film and stops corroding, a state engineers call passive.
The concrete is not merely armor.
It is a chemical environment that keeps the bar from rusting.
Air undoes this slowly.
Carbon dioxide dissolves in the pore water and reacts with the calcium hydroxide to make calcium carbonate.
Carbonated concrete is slightly harder and slightly denser.
What it has lost is alkalinity: the pH behind the carbonation front falls below about nine.
As long as unreacted portlandite remains the pH holds, so the portlandite acts as an alkaline reserve, a stock of protection that the air spends.
The front moves inward roughly in proportion to the square root of time, so a depth reached in ten years takes forty to double.
That arithmetic is the logic behind the specified cover, the twenty to fifty millimeters between the outer face and the nearest bar.
When the front reaches the steel, the film goes and the bar begins to rust.
Rust is the slow failure mode of the built environment, and it is mechanical as much as chemical: iron oxides occupy several times the volume of the metal they replace.
The expanding rust cracks the cover along the bar and pushes slabs of it off.
Chloride from sea spray or road salt does the same work faster and more locally, breaking the passive film in pits without waiting for the pH to fall.
A bridge deck rarely fails because the concrete was crushed.
It fails because the steel inside it grew.
Because the carbon is in the limestone, the most direct way to cut emissions is to use less clinker.
Industry has long done this by blending in supplementary materials, cementitious or pozzolanic.
Fly ash from coal boilers and slag from blast furnaces both react with water and lime to make more C-S-H.
A newer blend grinds together clinker, limestone, and clay calcined at roughly eight hundred degrees, too cool to decompose carbonate, and can replace about half the clinker.
Roman builders made durable marine mortar from lime and volcanic ash on much the same principle, with no steel in it, and some of their harbor works still stand.
The catch is chemical, and it deserves more attention than it usually gets.
A pozzolan makes its extra glue by consuming calcium hydroxide.
The reaction that adds strength is the one that spends the alkaline reserve, so a binder with less portlandite has less protection to give the steel when the carbonation front arrives.
Against that, the same blends usually produce a finer, less connected pore structure, which slows carbon dioxide on its way in.
Which effect wins is not a matter of principle but of the mix, the cover, the curing, and the exposure, and for a given structure it has to be worked out rather than assumed.
Supply is the other limit.
Fly ash and slag exist because coal is burned and iron is smelted, so the two established substitutes are byproducts of other high-carbon industries and grow scarcer as those clean up or close down.
Suitable clay is common almost everywhere, but a plant has to be built to calcine it.
Other routes are under development, none yet ordinary.
Capturing carbon dioxide at the kiln stack would address process and fuel emissions together, at a cost in energy and equipment.
Binders based on magnesium or alkali-activated slag avoid the limestone problem and raise their own unsettled questions.
Underneath all of it sits an accounting question.
Emissions are counted per tonne of cement, but service is counted in years.

A binder that cuts emissions by a third and halves the structure's life has gained nothing, because the replacement pour will emit again, and a plain mix with generous cover and patient curing may beat a clever one that is rushed.
The chemistry of concrete is not a problem waiting for one substitute.
It is a set of trades among the heat that makes the binder, the water that grows it, and the air that slowly spends it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, calcination is the step in which
choices: limestone sheds its carbon dioxide and becomes quicklime
the clay contributes the silica, alumina, and iron the kiln will need
gypsum is interground so the aluminate will not stiffen the batch too quickly
the ground powder meets water and begins precipitating the binding solid
quicklime and silica fuse and crystallize into gravel-sized nodules

proof.quote: the limestone gives up its carbon dioxide and becomes calcium oxide, or quicklime
This step is called calcination

questions.why: Paragraph 2 names this step outright. Near nine hundred degrees the limestone loses its carbon dioxide and becomes calcium oxide, or quicklime, and the passage calls that calcination.
distractorNotes: The clay does supply those oxides, but that is the makeup of the raw meal, not the reaction the passage names.
Interground gypsum belongs to paragraph 4, after the clinker has already been made and cooled.
That is hydration, which happens once water is added on the job, not inside the kiln.
That is the hotter clinkering step farther down the kiln, which paragraph 3 treats separately.

questions.stem: The passage indicates that gypsum is ground in with the clinker in order to
choices: give the finished powder its characteristic gray color
hold water in the mix so that hydration can continue for longer
raise the proportion of alite so the cement gains strength sooner
keep the tricalcium aluminate from stiffening the batch almost at once
replace part of the clinker and lower the emissions of the finished cement

proof.quote: the tricalcium aluminate would react within minutes and seize the batch

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says the gypsum is not filler. Without it the tricalcium aluminate would react within minutes and seize the batch, a failure the passage calls flash set.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 3 credits the gray color to the calcium aluminoferrite phase, not to the gypsum.
Keeping water available is curing, which paragraph 7 puts in the hands of the crew after the concrete is placed.
Alite content is set in the kiln, and paragraph 6 treats early strength as a matter of clinker composition rather than anything gypsum does.
That describes the supplementary materials of paragraph 12, while the three to five percent of gypsum is there to control setting.

questions.stem: According to the passage, most of the strength a concrete gains in its first week comes from
choices: alite, the most abundant phase in clinker
the calcium aluminoferrite that colors the powder
belite, the slower of the two calcium silicates
portlandite crystallizing out of the pore water
ettringite needles built around the cement grains

proof.quote: supplies most of the strength gained in the first week
makes up half to two thirds of the clinker

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says the two silicates set the pace and gives the first week to alite. Paragraph 3 has already put alite at half to two thirds of the clinker.
distractorNotes: The ferrite phase is mentioned only for the gray color it gives the powder.
Belite is the other silicate, but the passage gives it months and years rather than the first week.
Portlandite is released by the reaction, and paragraph 5 says plainly that it is not much of a glue.
Ettringite is what slows the aluminate down so the batch stays workable, and the passage never calls it a source of strength.

questions.stem: The passage puts the pH of the pore water in sound hardened concrete closest to

proof.quote: between about twelve and a half and thirteen and a half

questions.why: Paragraph 9 gives a range of about twelve and a half to thirteen and a half for the pore water, and thirteen is the only value here inside it.
distractorNotes: That is acidic, the opposite of the strongly alkaline liquid paragraph 9 describes.
Neutral water would not grow the protective film, and the passage stresses how alkaline the pore water is.
Below about nine is the value paragraph 10 gives for concrete that has already carbonated.
The passage tops the range out near thirteen and a half, not at the extreme end of the scale.

questions.stem: For every tonne of clinker produced, the passage says the limestone itself gives off about
choices: eight tenths of a tonne of carbon dioxide
half a tonne of carbon dioxide
a full tonne of carbon dioxide
a fifth of a tonne of carbon dioxide
seven or eight percent of a tonne of carbon dioxide

proof.quote: Roughly half a tonne of carbon dioxide leaves the limestone

questions.why: Paragraph 8 separates two sources. Roughly half a tonne comes out of the rock as stoichiometry alone, before any fuel is counted.
distractorNotes: That is the total once the fuel for firing and the energy for grinding are added in, not the share from the rock.
The passage keeps the share from the limestone well under a tonne, at roughly half.
The passage never gives this figure, and it would make the share coming from the rock look far smaller than it is.
Seven or eight percent is cement's share of human carbon dioxide emissions, a different figure entirely.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 7, "green" most nearly means
choices: inexperienced or newly trained
rich in plant material or organic matter
freshly placed and not yet hardened
produced with unusually low emissions
tinted by the iron in the clinker

proof.quote: soft enough to take a thumbprint and not yet carrying load

questions.why: Paragraph 7 defines the word in the same sentence: soft enough to take a thumbprint and not yet carrying load. It describes how young the pour is.
distractorNotes: That is the everyday sense of the word, and it does not fit a sentence about a slab that still takes a thumbprint.
Nothing organic is involved, since the passage is describing cement, sand, stone, and water.
Emissions do come up, but not until paragraph 8, and here the word describes a slab that has just been placed.
Paragraph 3 credits the gray color to the ferrite phase, and nothing in the passage is green in color.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 10, "reserve" most nearly means
choices: a rule written into a specification
a spare batch held back for repairs
an area of land protected from building
a cautious, understated manner
a stored supply that gets used up

proof.quote: a stock of protection that the air spends

questions.why: Paragraph 10 supplies the sense itself: the portlandite is a stock of protection that the air spends. It is an amount on hand that carbonation draws down.
distractorNotes: Cover depth is specified later in the paragraph, but the reserve is a quantity of portlandite rather than a written requirement.
Nothing is being held back for later, since the portlandite is already in place and is consumed where it sits.
The land sense is a real dictionary meaning, but the passage is describing a chemical stock inside the concrete.
That is the personality sense of the word, which has no place in a sentence about how long the pH holds.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which statement about a fresh slab left uncovered on a hot, dry day?
choices: It will carbonate before its steel has a chance to become passive
It will never set at all, since the cement cannot react without cover
It may stop gaining strength while some of its cement is still unreacted
It needs a larger share of gypsum to make up for the water it has lost to the air
It will set faster and therefore end up stronger than one kept damp

proof.quote: hydration stops when the water runs out, whether or not the surface looks dry
most easily ruined by a hot dry afternoon

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says hydration stops when the water runs out, whether or not the surface looks dry. A slab that loses its water early leaves cement unreacted and stops gaining.
distractorNotes: Carbonation belongs to paragraph 10 and works over years, not over a single afternoon.
Hydration starts as soon as water is added, so the slab does set. The passage says the reaction stops early, not that it never begins.
Gypsum controls how fast the aluminate reacts, and the passage never ties it to how much water a slab keeps.
This is the intuition the paragraph is written to correct, since drying is not hardening and losing water early costs strength.

questions.stem: The passage best supports which inference about the Roman marine mortar it mentions?
choices: It was fired in kilns that reached the same temperature as a modern clinker kiln
It was immune to carbonation because volcanic ash blocks carbon dioxide entirely
Its long life shows that lime and ash binders are stronger than any modern cement
A loss of alkalinity would not have threatened it as it threatens modern members
Roman builders had worked out why steel stays passive in alkaline surroundings

proof.quote: some of their harbor works still stand
has less protection to give the steel
It is a chemical environment that keeps the bar from rusting.

questions.why: Paragraph 12 describes a binder of lime and volcanic ash, and paragraph 9 explains that alkalinity matters because of the steel cast inside modern concrete. A mortar with no steel in it has nothing for a falling pH to endanger.
distractorNotes: Only the Portland kiln is given a temperature, about fourteen hundred and fifty degrees, and Roman firing is never described.
Nothing in the passage says volcanic ash blocks carbon dioxide, and paragraph 13 says only that finer pores slow it down.
The passage calls the mortar durable, which is a claim about lasting rather than about out-performing modern cement in strength.
The passive film is presented as modern engineering language, and the passage credits the Romans with a working principle instead.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central point of the passage?
choices: Concrete is overused, and the volume poured each year ought to be cut sharply
Corrosion of reinforcing steel is the leading cause of building collapse worldwide
Ancient builders understood durability far better than modern engineers manage to
Blended binders have made ordinary Portland cement obsolete for new construction
One chemistry sets cement's usefulness, its carbon cost, and its slow decay

proof.quote: the source of both the usefulness and the trouble of cement
not a problem waiting for one substitute
a set of trades among the heat that makes the binder

questions.why: The passage follows one chain. The calcination that makes the binder is the step that releases the carbon dioxide, and the portlandite that protects the steel is the compound the air slowly spends. Every proposal at the end is weighed against that chain.
distractorNotes: The passage never argues for building less, and the closing paragraph is about how binders should be compared.
Rust is called the slow failure mode of the built environment, which is not the same as a worldwide count of collapses.
The Roman mortar appears once to illustrate a principle, not as a verdict on modern engineering.
Paragraph 13 presents the blends as a trade with an unsettled outcome, not as a replacement that has already won.

choices: correct a common misunderstanding and show what it costs
compare the two calcium silicates that set the pace
introduce the carbonation reaction that arrives later on
explain why cement kilns have to be fired so hot
show that site crews are careless with the mixes they place

proof.quote: Here the common intuition fails.
Concrete does not harden by drying out.
Those pores are where strength goes

questions.why: The paragraph opens by saying the common intuition fails, replaces drying with hydration, and then follows the error to the extra water and the capillary pores it leaves behind.
distractorNotes: That comparison is the work of paragraph 6, which comes just before this one.
Carbonation is introduced in paragraph 10. What paragraph 7 introduces is the pore network that later lets it in.
Kiln temperature is handled in paragraphs 2 and 3, while paragraph 7 is about what happens after the cement leaves the plant.
The passage explains that a wetter mix is easier to place, describing the tradeoff rather than faulting anyone for it.

questions.stem: The passage is organized mainly by
choices: opening with a failure and working backward to its causes
moving through the four clinker phases one at a time
setting ancient construction against modern construction throughout
following the material forward in time, then testing proposals against it
alternating a chemical claim with a rebuttal of that claim in every paragraph

proof.quote: The story starts in a quarry and a kiln.
Add water and the real reaction begins.
Air undoes this slowly.
Other routes are under development, none yet ordinary.

questions.why: The passage runs quarry, kiln, clinker, hydration, curing, then emissions and decades of slow carbonation. Only after all that does it take up substitutes, supply, and the accounting.
distractorNotes: The failure arrives late, in paragraphs 10 and 11, after the chemistry that explains it has been laid out.
The four phases are named once, in paragraph 3, and two of them are barely mentioned again.
Roman mortar occupies a single sentence rather than framing the whole passage.
There is pushback in paragraphs 7 and 13, but most paragraphs simply carry the account forward.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the carbon dioxide that comes out of the limestone is best described as
choices: matter of fact about an unavoidable piece of chemistry
indignant at an industry that has refused to act
confident that cleaner fuel will shortly remove the whole problem
dismissive of a figure that is often exaggerated
puzzled by a source of emissions nobody has explained

proof.quote: a problem no engineer can design away
purely as stoichiometry

questions.why: Paragraph 8 calls it a problem no engineer can design away and explains it as stoichiometry. The author gives the size of it plainly, without blaming anyone or promising a fix.
distractorNotes: The paragraph assigns no blame and says instead that the carbon was in the rock to begin with.
Fuel is only part of the total, and the passage says more than half of the emissions are chemical rather than combustion.
The author treats the figure as serious, comparing cement's share with that of aviation.
The origin is explained exactly, in one sentence about where the carbon was.

questions.stem: In paragraph 13, the author's attitude toward blended binders is best described as
choices: openly enthusiastic about a settled improvement
interested but unwilling to generalize from principle
resigned to the idea that nothing much can be improved here
hostile, on the grounds that they endanger structures
indifferent to which binder a given project chooses

proof.quote: not a matter of principle but of the mix
has to be worked out rather than assumed

questions.why: Paragraph 13 gives the blends a real benefit, a finer pore structure, and a real cost, a smaller alkaline reserve, then says which effect wins has to be worked out for the particular mix and exposure.
distractorNotes: The paragraph opens with a catch and never treats the question as settled.
The author is weighing an option rather than giving one up, and the closing paragraph still looks for better practice.
The danger is conditional here, and the same paragraph credits the blends with slowing carbon dioxide down.
Indifference would not fit a paragraph that says the catch deserves more attention than it usually gets.

questions.stem: The passage supports each of the following statements EXCEPT:
choices: Chloride can break the protective film without any fall in pH
Carbonated concrete is denser than the concrete it formed from
Concrete reaches its final strength once its surface is dry
Belite goes on adding strength for months after a structure is finished
Cover depth is specified because the carbonation front advances slowly

proof.quote: keeps adding strength for months and years
without waiting for the pH to fall
slightly harder and slightly denser
That arithmetic is the logic behind the specified cover
whether or not the surface looks dry
a structure quietly gets stronger long after the forms come off

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says the opposite. Water is a reactant, and hydration stops when the water runs out, whether or not the surface looks dry, so a dry surface is not a finished reaction.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 11 says chloride breaks the film in pits without waiting for the pH to fall, so this one is supported.
Paragraph 10 calls carbonated concrete slightly harder and slightly denser, so this one is supported.
Paragraph 6 gives belite months and years of continued gain, so this one is supported.
Paragraph 10 ties the specified cover to a front that advances with the square root of time, so this one is supported.

questions.stem: A reader looking for the reason a very large dam might be built with a slow-gaining cement would find it in which paragraph?
choices: Paragraph 4
Paragraph 5
Paragraph 6
Paragraph 10
Paragraph 13

proof.quote: an advantage in a massive dam

questions.why: Paragraph 6 contrasts the two silicates and closes on the dam: a cement heavier in belite runs cool, and the heat of reaction would otherwise crack a mass that size as it cooled.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 4 is about gypsum and flash set, a matter of minutes rather than of heat in a massive pour.
Paragraph 5 describes hydration and names its products, but the dam example is not there.
Paragraph 10 covers carbonation and cover depth, long after any heat of reaction has gone.
Paragraph 13 weighs blended binders and says nothing about heat in a large pour.
